description: Anglo-Norman and English lordship (1171–1541) established by Henry II's expedition; its actual control rarely extended beyond the Pale around Dublin, while successive English absentee lords and native Irish resistance produced the 'degenerate English' phenomenon, colonists who culturally assimilated to Gaelic ways, making Ireland a perpetual drain on English resources and a source of constitutional innovation in the concept of overseas lordship.

lifecycle_phases.description: Henry II of England declares himself Lord of Ireland (1171–1172), following the Norman mercenary invasion invited by Dermot MacMurrough. His son John (later King John) is made Lord of Ireland (1177). Anglo-Norman lords (de Clare, de Burgh, le Gros) carve out substantial lordships while Gaelic Irish kings survive in the west and north. The Statutes of Kilkenny (1366) later attempt to prevent Anglo-Norman assimilation into Irish culture.

The Anglo-Norman settlement contracts to the 'Pale' around Dublin and a few coastal towns as Gaelic Ireland reasserts itself. The Bruce invasion (1315–1318) briefly threatens English control. By 1500, the Earl of Kildare (Fitzgerald family) runs Ireland as a de facto autonomous lord, barely acknowledging English authority. The 'mere English' become 'more Irish than the Irish themselves.'

rise_factors.description: Norman castle-building and heavy cavalry tactics were decisive against Irish infantry and chariot warfare; the combination of motte-and-bailey castles and mounted knights allowed rapid pacification of the lowlands

Grants of Irish land to Anglo-Norman magnates (de Lacy, Marshal, de Burgh) created a feudal network in eastern Ireland; Dublin as an administrative center and the Pale as a defended English zone maintained an effective, if limited, English presence

Richard de Clare (Strongbow)'s invasion (1169–70), invited by Diarmait Mac Murchada, established Norman control of Leinster. Henry II's subsequent arrival (1171) turned a private Norman conquest into an English royal lordship, though direct control remained limited.

Ireland exported wool, hides, and cattle to English and continental markets. The Pale (English-controlled eastern zone) developed as an agricultural surplus area feeding English urban markets, providing economic rationale for continued English presence.

Pope Adrian IV's bull Laudabiliter (1155) granted Henry II of England lordship over Ireland; his actual expedition in 1171–72 established the basis for English governance with Irish kings rendering formal submission.

The English colonial network established new walled boroughs, Kilkenny, Cork, Waterford, Drogheda, that channeled Irish agricultural exports through English-controlled ports generating customs revenues that funded the Lordship's administration.

decline_factors.description: Anglo-Norman lords in Ireland rapidly became independent of English royal control, adopting Irish customs, law, and alliances; the 'degenerate English' who 'went native' undermined the project of English governance from within

The Black Death hit English settlements hardest; Gaelic lords recovered land and independence in the 14th century; by 1400 English control was limited to the Pale around Dublin; the Statutes of Kilkenny (1366) acknowledged the failure of cultural assimilation

English lords with Irish holdings prioritized English politics and estates; lords-lieutenant changed frequently; the lack of sustained royal attention allowed Anglo-Norman families (the Old English) to become semi-autonomous Gaelic lords themselves

The area of effective English control contracted throughout the 14th–15th centuries to a shrinking "Pale" around Dublin, with the Statutes of Kilkenny (1366) demonstrating how thoroughly Gaelic culture had re-established itself beyond English jurisdiction.
